title: Rabin-Karp and Rolling Hash
summary: Rabin-Karp turns substring comparison into number comparison by hashing each window as a polynomial, then rolling that hash forward in O(1) per character — with collision-safe verification and multi-pattern search built in.

slides.markdown:
**Rabin-Karp** solves the same problem as [naive-pattern-matching-and-kmp](naive-pattern-matching-and-kmp) — find a pattern inside a text — with a completely different idea: turn each candidate substring into a single number (a hash), and compare *numbers* instead of *characters*.

The trick that makes this fast is the **rolling hash**: sliding the comparison window one character to the right lets you compute the new window's hash from the old one in O(1), without rehashing from scratch. That gives an average-case O(n + m), with a worst case that still needs a safety net — hash collisions are real, and Rabin-Karp's correctness depends on always verifying a hash match with an actual character comparison.

slides.sectionTitle: A substring as a base-B number
slides.markdown:
Treat a string as digits of a number in some base B (say, B = 256 for byte values, or 26 for lowercase letters). The string `"abc"` becomes the polynomial:

`hash("abc") = a·B² + b·B¹ + c·B⁰` (using each character's numeric code for a, b, c)

Every substring of a fixed length m maps to one such number, computed modulo some large prime to keep it from overflowing. Two equal substrings always produce equal hashes — this direction is guaranteed. The reverse — equal hashes implying equal substrings — is only *probable*, not guaranteed, which is exactly why Rabin-Karp always double-checks a hash match against the real characters.

```python
def window_hash(s, base, mod):
    h = 0
    for ch in s:
        h = (h * base + ord(ch)) % mod
    return h

# initial hash of the pattern, and of the text's first window
MOD = 1_000_000_007
BASE = 256
pattern_hash = window_hash(pattern, BASE, MOD)
window_hash_val = window_hash(text[:m], BASE, MOD)
```

This costs O(m) — the same as computing the first hash directly. The saving comes entirely from the *next* step: sliding the window without redoing this full computation.

slides.sectionTitle: Sliding the window one character right
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a text string with a highlighted window of length 4 at position i, and the same window shifted to position i+1; annotate the leftmost character of the old window (leaving the window, with a minus sign) and the new rightmost character entering (with a plus sign); show the polynomial terms shifting: each remaining character's positional weight increases by one power of the base, and the new character enters at weight B^0 >>>

The picture is the whole idea: moving the window right doesn't touch m-1 characters that are still inside the window in spirit — it only needs to remove the departing character's contribution and add the arriving one's, at the correct power of the base.

Rolling forward means three arithmetic moves: subtract the leaving character's weighted contribution, multiply by the base (shifting every remaining term up one power), then add the new character's contribution.

Formally: `new_hash = (old_hash - text[i]·B^(m-1))·B + text[i+m]`, all taken modulo the chosen prime. Every one of those is a constant number of multiplications, subtractions, and additions — no matter how large the window is, rolling forward always costs the same O(1). That's the entire speed argument: after the first O(m) hash, every subsequent window is O(1), for a total of O(n) across the whole text.

```python
def rabin_karp(text, pattern, base=256, mod=1_000_000_007):
    n, m = len(text), len(pattern)
    if m > n:
        return []
    high_order = pow(base, m - 1, mod)
    p_hash = window_hash(pattern, base, mod)
    t_hash = window_hash(text[:m], base, mod)
    matches = []

    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        if p_hash == t_hash and text[i:i+m] == pattern:   # verify, never trust the hash alone
            matches.append(i)
        if i < n - m:
            t_hash = (t_hash - ord(text[i]) * high_order) % mod
            t_hash = (t_hash * base + ord(text[i + m])) % mod
            t_hash %= mod   # keep it non-negative
    return matches
```

Note the verification step — `text[i:i+m] == pattern` — runs *only* when the hashes already match, so it almost never fires on a well-chosen modulus, keeping the average case close to O(n + m).

slides.sectionTitle: Hash collisions are real — always verify
slides.markdown:
Two different substrings can hash to the same value — a **collision**. With a good modulus this is rare, but "rare" is not "impossible," and an interview or a production system that skips verification is silently wrong on exactly the inputs where it matters most (an adversary can, in principle, construct a collision on a known modulus).

The fix is the one line easy to skip under time pressure: whenever hashes match, do a direct character comparison before reporting a match. That comparison only runs on the (rare) hash collisions, so it doesn't change the average-case complexity, but it's the difference between an algorithm that's *usually* right and one that's *always* right.

The modulus should be a **large prime** — commonly something near 10⁹ or larger — chosen so that the product `base × mod` still fits comfortably in the integer type you're using (or so that intermediate products don't silently overflow in a fixed-width language). A prime modulus spreads hash values more evenly across buckets than a composite one, lowering collision odds.

The base should exceed the size of your character set (256 safely covers any byte value; 31 or 26 is common for lowercase-only problems) so distinct characters map to genuinely distinct digit values.

A common hardening trick: run **two independent hashes** with different (base, mod) pairs and require both to match before verifying with a direct comparison — collapses the collision probability to the product of both individual probabilities, which is effectively zero in practice.

Rabin-Karp generalizes cleanly to searching for **many patterns at once**: hash every pattern once up front into a set (or map, if you need to know which pattern matched), then scan the text a single time, rolling the window hash forward and checking set membership at each position.

This is the string-hashing equivalent of the shared-trie trick in [trie-applications](trie-applications) — instead of running one search per pattern, one pass over the text answers "does any pattern match here" for all patterns simultaneously, provided all patterns share the same length (mixed-length patterns need one pass per distinct length, or a different structure entirely).

| | Rabin-Karp | KMP |
|---|---|---|
| Average case | O(n + m) | O(n + m) |
| Worst case | O(n·m) if collisions are adversarially forced | O(n + m), always |
| Extra structure | A rolling hash, a modulus and base choice | The LPS array |
| Multi-pattern search | Natural — hash all patterns into a set, one text pass | Needs a separate structure (e.g. Aho-Corasick) |
| Conceptual complexity | Simple idea, subtle correctness (collisions, modular arithmetic) | Trickier idea, no probabilistic caveat once built |

Reach for Rabin-Karp when you need multi-pattern search or 2D pattern matching (hashing rows/blocks) — its hashing model generalizes there more naturally than KMP's character-by-character bookkeeping. Reach for KMP when you need a hard worst-case guarantee with no probabilistic caveat at all.

The roll step subtracts a term before re-multiplying: `(old_hash - departing_term) * base + arriving_term`. In languages where `%` can return a negative result for a negative operand (C, C++, Java, JavaScript — Python's `%` is the exception, always returning non-negative), that subtraction can produce a negative intermediate value, and taking `% mod` on a negative number doesn't automatically wrap it back into `[0, mod)`.

The fix is defensive: add `mod` before taking the modulus, i.e. `((old_hash - departing_term) % mod + mod) % mod`. Skipping this doesn't crash — it silently produces a negative hash that will never again equal any legitimately-computed positive hash, so matches quietly stop being found from that point in the scan onward.
